claim: In the striatum, AC5 exists in a stable pre-coupled complex with subunits of Golf heterotrimer.
source: In this study, we report that in the striatum AC5 exists in a stable pre-coupled complex with subunits of Golf heterotrimer.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing AC5 binding to Gαolf and Gβ2 in striatal lysates (Figure 1A).

claim: AC5 was effectively and specifically pulled down together with both Gαolf and Gβ2 from mouse striatal lysates.
source: AC5 was effectively and specifically pulled down together with both Gαolf and, to a lesser extent, Gβ2 from mouse striatal lysates, indicating that in striatal neurons Golf subunits form stable complexes with AC5 in their ground state in the absence of receptor stimulation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct experimental observation from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Golf subunits form stable complexes with AC5 in their ground state in the absence of receptor stimulation.
source: AC5 was effectively and specifically pulled down together with both Gαolf and, to a lesser extent, Gβ2 from mouse striatal lysates, indicating that in striatal neurons Golf subunits form stable complexes with AC5 in their ground state in the absence of receptor stimulation (Figure 1A).
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data showing complex formation without agonist stimulation.

claim: Elimination of AC5 in mice dramatically reduced the expression of Gαolf.
source: Elimination of AC5 in mice (Adcy5-/-) dramatically reduced the expression of Gαolf but had no appreciable effect on Gβ2 expression, suggesting that AC5 contributes to the stability of Gαolf but not the stability of the Gβ2γ7 complex (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting analysis of Adcy5-/- mice showing reduced Gαolf levels (Figure 1B).

claim: AC5 contributes to the stability of Gαolf but not the stability of the Gβ2γ7 complex.
source: Elimination of AC5 in mice (Adcy5-/-) dramatically reduced the expression of Gαolf but had no appreciable effect on Gβ2 expression, suggesting that AC5 contributes to the stability of Gαolf but not the stability of the Gβ2γ7 complex (Figure 1B).
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of AC5 knockout on Gαolf versus Gβ2 expression levels.

claim: Disruption of Gβ2γ7 by eliminating Gγ7 led to a marked down-regulation of both AC5 and Gαolf expression.
source: In contrast, disruption of Gβ2γ7 by eliminating Gγ7 in Gng7-/- knockout led to a marked down-regulation of both AC5 and Gαolf expression (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting analysis of Gng7-/- mice (Figure 1D).

claim: In Gnal+/- mice with reduced Gαolf expression, the levels of both AC5 and Gβ2 were substantially reduced.
source: In these animals, the levels of both AC5 and Gβ2 were substantially reduced (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting analysis of Gnal+/- mice (Figure 1E).

claim: Complete ablation of Gαolf leads to increased perinatal lethality.
source: The consequences of Gαolf disruption were evaluated in heterozygous mice (Gnal+/-) with severely diminished Gαolf expression because complete ablation of Gαolf leads to increased perinatal lethality (Belluscio et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Belluscio et al., 1998.

claim: Co-dependence of the Golf-AC5 complex components is unidirectional: destabilization of either Gα or Gβγ subunits compromised AC5 stability, while only Gα but not Gβγ was affected by the loss of AC5.
source: Therefore, in mouse striatum co-dependence of the complex components appears to be unidirectional: destabilization of either the Gα or Gβγ subunits of the Golf heterotrimer compromised AC5 stability, while only Gα but not Gβγ was affected by the loss of AC5.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of multiple knockout experiments (Figures 1B, 1D, 1E).

claim: Co-expression with Gαolf dramatically increased levels of AC5 in HEK293 cells.
source: Consistent with the in vivo data, co-expression with Gαolf dramatically increased levels of AC5, and vice versa, the introduction of AC5 enhanced the expression of Gαolf (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by transfection experiments in HEK293 cells (Figure 1F).

claim: Introduction of AC5 enhanced the expression of Gαolf in HEK293 cells.
source: Consistent with the in vivo data, co-expression with Gαolf dramatically increased levels of AC5, and vice versa, the introduction of AC5 enhanced the expression of Gαolf (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by transfection experiments in HEK293 cells (Figure 1F).

claim: No significant changes in AC5 or Gβ2γ7 levels were observed upon their co-expression in HEK293 cells.
source: In contrast, no significant changes in AC5 or Gβ2γ7 levels were observed upon their co-expression (Figure 1G).
evidence: Demonstrated by transfection experiments in HEK293 cells (Figure 1G).

claim: Co-expression with Gαolf increased the levels of Gβ2γ7 in HEK293 cells.
source: We further observed co-dependence between Gαolf and Gβ2γ7 subunits in which co-expression with Gαolf increased the levels of Gβ2γ7 and co-expression of Gβ2γ7 enhanced levels Gαolf (Figure 1H).
evidence: Demonstrated by transfection experiments in HEK293 cells (Figure 1H).

claim: Co-expression of Gβ2γ7 enhanced levels of Gαolf in HEK293 cells.
source: We further observed co-dependence between Gαolf and Gβ2γ7 subunits in which co-expression with Gαolf increased the levels of Gβ2γ7 and co-expression of Gβ2γ7 enhanced levels Gαolf (Figure 1H).
evidence: Demonstrated by transfection experiments in HEK293 cells (Figure 1H).

claim: The association between components of the Golf-AC5 complex is required for its stability.
source: Collectively, these data strongly support the existence of a complex between AC5 and the Gαolfβ2γ7 heterotrimer and indicate that the association between components of this complex is required for its stability.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of knockout and transfection experiments showing mutual stabilization.

claim: PhLP1 has been described to serve as a co-factor for the assembly of signaling complexes containing β subunits of heterotrimeric G proteins.
source: In search of factors that may regulate the assembly of Golf-AC5 complex, our attention was drawn to phosducin like protein 1 (PhLP1), which has been described to serve as a co-factor for the assembly of signaling complexes containing β subunits of heterotrimeric G proteins (Willardson and Tracy, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Willardson and Tracy, 2012.

claim: Co-transfection with PhLP1 significantly increased the expression of all three Golf subunits in HEK293 cells.
source: In HEK293 cells, co-transfection with PhLP1 significantly increased the expression of all three Golf subunits (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by transfection experiments in HEK293 cells (Figure 2A).

claim: A dominant negative construct of PhLP1 (ΔNT-PhLP1), lacking the first 75 amino acids critical for its interaction with Gβ, had no effect on the expression of Golf subunits.
source: In contrast, a dominant negative construct of PhLP1 (ΔNT-PhLP1), lacking the first 75 amino acids critical for its interaction with Gβ (Lukov et al., 2005) had no effect on the expression Golf subunits (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by transfection experiments in HEK293 cells (Figure 2A) and supported by citation to Lukov et al., 2005.

claim: Co-expression with full-length PhLP1 resulted in a significant increase in the formation of the Gβ2γ7 complexes.
source: Consistent with the described impact of PhLP1 on Gβγ complexes (Lukov et al., 2005), co-expression with full-length PhLP1 resulted in a significant increase in the formation of the Gβ2γ7 complexes as evidenced by the fluorescence complementation assay with the split-Venus system (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence complementation assay (Figure 2B) and supported by citation to Lukov et al., 2005.

claim: ΔNT-PhLP1 inhibited Gβ2γ7 assembly.
source: In contrast, ΔNT-PhLP1 exerted the opposite effect and inhibited Gβ2γ7 assembly (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence complementation assay (Figure 2B).

claim: PhLP1 coexpression significantly increased dopamine-induced activation of Gαolf-Gβ2γ7 heterotrimer.
source: Using this assay we found that PhLP1 coexpression significantly increased dopamine-induced activation of Gαolf-Gβ2γ7 heterotrimer (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Demonstrated by BRET assay in HEK293 cells (Figures 2F and 2G).

claim: Expression of the dominant negative ΔNT-PhLP1 significantly attenuated the BRET response.
source: In contrast, expression of the dominant negative ΔNT-PhLP1 significantly attenuated the BRET response (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Demonstrated by BRET assay in HEK293 cells (Figures 2F and 2G).

claim: PhLP1 facilitates functional coupling of GαolfGβ2γ7 to D1 receptors.
source: These observations suggest that PhLP1 facilitates functional coupling of GαolfGβ2γ7 to D1 receptors, likely owning to its ability to promote the assembly of Gβ2γ7 complexes.
evidence: Inferred from BRET assay results showing enhanced D1R-mediated activation.

claim: PhLP1 co-expression resulted in a significant increase (~1.7 fold) in AC5 expression in HEK293 cells.
source: PhLP1 co-expression resulted in a significant increase (~1.7 fold) in AC5 expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by transfection experiments in HEK293 cells (Figure 3A).

claim: PhLP1 overexpression elevated basal cAMP levels (~4 fold) in cells expressing AC5.
source: This effect was paralleled by elevation of the basal cAMP levels (~4 fold) in the cells expressing AC5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by cAMP measurements in transfected HEK293 cells (Figure 3B).

claim: AC5-containing cells showed enhanced cAMP generation in response to forskolin (~4 fold increase) when PhLP1 was overexpressed.
source: In addition, AC5-containing cells showed enhanced cAMP generation in response to both the direct AC activator forskolin (~4 fold increase) and the β2-adrenergic agonist isoproterenol (~1.5 fold increase) when PhLP1 was overexpressed (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by cAMP measurements in transfected HEK293 cells (Figure 3B).

claim: AC5-containing cells showed enhanced cAMP generation in response to isoproterenol (~1.5 fold increase) when PhLP1 was overexpressed.
source: In addition, AC5-containing cells showed enhanced cAMP generation in response to both the direct AC activator forskolin (~4 fold increase) and the β2-adrenergic agonist isoproterenol (~1.5 fold increase) when PhLP1 was overexpressed (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by cAMP measurements in transfected HEK293 cells (Figure 3B).

claim: No stimulatory effect on cAMP generation was observed in the absence of AC5 when PhLP1 was overexpressed.
source: These effects were AC5-dependent as no stimulatory effect on cAMP generation was observed in the absence of AC5 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by cAMP measurements in transfected HEK293 cells without AC5 (Figure 3C).

claim: Purified recombinant full-length PhLP1 significantly enhanced basal AC activity in striatal membranes.
source: Remarkably, purified recombinant full-length PhLP1 significantly enhanced basal AC activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by adenylyl cyclase activity assays using striatal membranes (Figure 3D).

claim: ΔNT-PhLP1 did not enhance basal AC activity in striatal membranes.
source: This effect was not observed with ΔNT-PhLP1, suggesting that the effect likely involves an ability of PhLP1 to bind Gβγ.
evidence: Demonstrated by adenylyl cyclase activity assays using striatal membranes (Figure 3D).

claim: PhLP1 significantly enhanced forskolin-stimulated AC activity in striatal membranes.
source: Consistent with our model, PhLP1 significantly enhanced forskolin-stimulated AC activity in striatal membranes and produced an approximately three-fold reduction in EC50 for forskolin (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by adenylyl cyclase activity assays using striatal membranes (Figures 3E and 3F).

claim: PhLP1 produced an approximately three-fold reduction in EC50 for forskolin in striatal membranes.
source: Consistent with our model, PhLP1 significantly enhanced forskolin-stimulated AC activity in striatal membranes and produced an approximately three-fold reduction in EC50 for forskolin (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by dose-response analysis in adenylyl cyclase activity assays (Figures 3E and 3F).

claim: PhLP1 failed to exert an effect on AC activated by adding exogenous Gαs-GTPγS.
source: In contrast, PhLP1 failed to exert an effect on AC activated by adding exogenous Gαs-GTPγS (Figure 3E and G) supporting the idea that PhLP1 activates AC5 through a Gα-dependent mechanism.
evidence: Demonstrated by adenylyl cyclase activity assays using striatal membranes (Figures 3E and 3G).

claim: PhLP1 activates AC5 through a Gα-dependent mechanism.
source: In contrast, PhLP1 failed to exert an effect on AC activated by adding exogenous Gαs-GTPγS (Figure 3E and G) supporting the idea that PhLP1 activates AC5 through a Gα-dependent mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of PhLP1 on forskolin versus Gαs-GTPγS stimulated AC activity.

claim: PhLP1 regulates AC5 activity by a dual mechanism: enhancing AC5 expression by facilitating complex formation with Golf, and promoting receptor-independent release of Gαolf that stimulates AC5 activity.
source: Thus, PhLP1 appears to regulate AC5 activity by a dual mechanism. On the one hand it enhances the expression of the AC5 by facilitating its complex formation with Golf. On the other, it may act in promoting the receptor-independent release of Gαolf that stimulates AC5 activity.
evidence: Inferred from combined results of expression studies and activity assays.

claim: PhLP1 protein is abundantly expressed in the mouse striatum.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Schroder and Lohse, 2000), we found PhLP1 protein to be abundantly expressed in the mouse striatum by immunoblotting (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting (Figure 4A) and supported by citation to Schroder and Lohse, 2000.

claim: Overall striatal morphology of Pdcl cKO mice looked normal with no signs of degeneration at least until 3–4 months of age.
source: Overall, striatal morphology of Pdcl cKO mice looked normal with no signs of degeneration at least until 3–4 months of age (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis (Figure 4C).

claim: Morphometric analysis revealed a decrease in the total volume of striatal tissue in Pdcl cKO mice.
source: Morphometric analysis revealed a decrease in the total volume of striatal tissue in Pdcl cKO mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by morphometric analysis (Figure 4D).

claim: Counting the number of neurons in the striatum tissue revealed a significantly greater number of neurons in the Pdcl cKO mice.
source: Counting the number of neurons (diameter > 5 μm) in the striatum tissue using Nissl staining revealed a significantly greater number of neurons in the Pdcl cKO mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by neuron counting from Nissl-stained sections (Figure 4D).

claim: The sizes of individual striatal neurons are likely smaller in Pdcl cKO mice.
source: A greater number of cells together with a smaller volume that they occupy indicate that the sizes of individual striatal neurons are likely smaller.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of increased neuron number and decreased striatal volume.

claim: The changes in striatal neuron size are consistent with retarded maturation of neurons, a process controlled by cAMP signaling.
source: These changes are consistent with retarded maturation of neurons, a process controlled by the cAMP signaling (Fujioka et al., 2004; Nakagawa et al., 2002).
evidence: Inferred from observed changes and supported by citations to Fujioka et al., 2004 and Nakagawa et al., 2002.

claim: Quantification of fluorescence intensity revealed no difference in the intensities of the signals for enkephalin and substance P markers in appropriate target areas.
source: Quantification of fluorescence intensity revealed no difference in the intensities of the signals for these markers, which were found in appropriate target areas (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis (Figure 4E).

claim: Loss of PhLP1 in the striatum does not lead to neuronal degeneration, but rather promotes neuronal survival while inhibiting their growth.
source: In summary, these data indicate that loss of PhLP1 in the striatum does not lead to neuronal degeneration, but rather promotes neuronal survival while inhibiting their growth.
evidence: Inferred from combined histological and morphometric analyses.

claim: The levels of PhLP1 protein were reduced by ~60% in Pdcl cKO striatum.
source: Immunoblotting shows that the levels of PhLP1 protein were reduced by ~60% in Pdcl cKO striatum.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting analysis (Figure 5A, 5B).

claim: The levels of Gαolf, Gβ2 and AC5 were severely reduced in Pdcl cKO striatum.
source: Consistent with the results in transfected cells, we found that the levels of Gαolf, Gβ2 and AC5 were severely reduced in Pdcl cKO as well.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting analysis (Figure 5A, 5B).

claim: Deletion of PhLP1 had a detrimental effect on the expression of Gβ5 and RGS9-2.
source: Deletion of PhLP1 also had a detrimental effect on the expression of Gβ5 and RGS9-2, as may have been expected from the studies on the rod and cone photoreceptors (Lai et al., 2013; Tracy et al., 2015).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting analysis (Figure 5A, 5B) and supported by citations to Lai et al., 2013 and Tracy et al., 2015.

claim: Deletion of PhLP1 did not affect the expression of Gβ1 and Gα subunits possibly associated with it: Gαo, Gαi, Gαq.
source: Interestingly, the effect was clearly selective as deletion of PhLP1 did not affect the expression of Gβ1 and Gα subunits possibly associated with it: Gαo, Gαi, Gαq (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting analysis (Figure 5B).

claim: The levels of RGS7 were unaffected by PhLP1 deletion.
source: Furthermore, the levels of another Gβ5 associated protein, RGS7 were also unaffected.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting analysis (Figure 5B).

claim: Analysis of the mRNA levels for corresponding down-regulated proteins showed no changes in the transcript levels.
source: Analysis of the mRNA levels for corresponding down-regulated proteins showed no changes in the transcript levels, suggesting that PhLP1 likely contributes to protein stability rather than affects the expression through a transcriptional mechanism (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by mRNA quantification (Figure 5C).

claim: PhLP1 likely contributes to protein stability rather than affects the expression through a transcriptional mechanism.
source: Analysis of the mRNA levels for corresponding down-regulated proteins showed no changes in the transcript levels, suggesting that PhLP1 likely contributes to protein stability rather than affects the expression through a transcriptional mechanism (Figure 5C).
evidence: Inferred from unchanged mRNA levels despite reduced protein levels.

claim: PhLP1 selectively affects biosynthesis and/or assembly of the AC5 signaling complex that contains GαolfGβ2γ7 and RGS9-2/Gβ5.
source: Therefore, it appears that PhLP1 selectively affects biosynthesis and/or assembly of the AC5 signaling complex that in addition to GαolfGβ2γ7 also contains RGS9-2/Gβ5 (Xie et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from selective effects on specific G protein subunits and supported by citation to Xie et al., 2012.

claim: Basal cAMP levels were substantially lower in the striatum tissues from Pdcl cKO mice as compared to their control littermates.
source: In agreement with the changes in protein levels, we found marked deficits in cAMP signaling. Basal cAMP levels were substantially lower in the striatum tissues from Pdcl cKO mice as compared to their control littermates (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by cAMP measurements in striatal tissues (Figure 5D).

claim: Adenylyl cyclase activity was lower in Pdcl cKO striatal membranes under both basal and forskolin-stimulated conditions.
source: Adenylyl cyclase activity measured with membranes isolated from the striatum was also lower upon the deletion of PhLP1 under both basal and forskolin-stimulated conditions (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by adenylyl cyclase activity assays (Figure 5E).

claim: The efficiency of D1R and A2AR coupling to cAMP production was lower in Pdcl cKO striatal membrane.
source: Finally, the efficiency of D1R and A2AR coupling to cAMP production was lower in Pdcl cKO striatal membrane (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by adenylyl cyclase activity assays with receptor agonists (Figure 5E).

claim: In the striatum PhLP1 is necessary for high-level expression of the AC5 complex components and its functional activity.
source: Together, these data indicate that in the striatum PhLP1 is necessary for high-level expression of the AC5 complex components and its functional activity.
evidence: Inferred from combined results of protein expression and functional activity assays.

claim: Pdcl cKO mice exhibited normal habituation to a novel environment.
source: In the open field test, Pdcl cKO mice exhibited normal habituation to a novel environment (Figure 6A) and had unaltered levels of basal locomotor activity as evidenced by both total distance traveled during the task (Figure 6B) and average locomotion velocity (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by open field test (Figure 6A).

claim: Pdcl cKO mice had unaltered levels of basal locomotor activity.
source: In the open field test, Pdcl cKO mice exhibited normal habituation to a novel environment (Figure 6A) and had unaltered levels of basal locomotor activity as evidenced by both total distance traveled during the task (Figure 6B) and average locomotion velocity (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by open field test measurements (Figures 6B and 6C).

claim: Pdcl cKO mice had normal thigmotaxis, stereotypy, pre-pulse inhibition and showed no signs of abnormal involuntary movements or clasping behavior.
source: The Pdcl cKO mice also had normal thigmotaxis, stereotypy, pre-pulse inhibition and showed no signs of abnormal involuntary movements or clasping behavior typically associated with gross striatal dysfunction (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as observed but data not shown.

claim: Mice of both genotypes that were naïve to the rotarod procedure performed equally during initial trial.
source: In the accelerating rotarod task, mice of both genotypes that were naïve to the procedure performed equally during initial trial, indicating their normal motor coordination (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by rotarod test (Figure 6D).

claim: While the performance of control littermates improved with each subsequent rotarod trial, Pdcl cKO mice performed at the same level during all trial sessions.
source: However, the behavior of Pdcl cKO mice was dramatically different when multiple trials were conducted. While the performance of control littermates improved with each subsequent trial, Pdcl cKO mice performed at the same level during all trial sessions (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by rotarod test (Figure 6D).

claim: Knockout of Pdcl in the striatum completely abolishes motor learning in mice.
source: These data indicate that knockout of Pdcl in the striatum completely abolishes motor learning in mice.
evidence: Inferred from rotarod test results showing lack of improvement across trials.

claim: Pdcl cKO mice showed enhanced forelimb grips strength.
source: Pdcl cKO mice also showed enhanced forelimb grips strength (Figure 6E) and augmented response to acoustic startle (Figure 6F), suggesting further deficits in processing sensorimotor stimuli.
evidence: Demonstrated by grip strength test (Figure 6E).

claim: Pdcl cKO mice showed augmented response to acoustic startle.
source: Pdcl cKO mice also showed enhanced forelimb grips strength (Figure 6E) and augmented response to acoustic startle (Figure 6F), suggesting further deficits in processing sensorimotor stimuli.
evidence: Demonstrated by acoustic startle test (Figure 6F).

claim: Pdcl cKO mice have deficits in processing sensorimotor stimuli.
source: Pdcl cKO mice also showed enhanced forelimb grips strength (Figure 6E) and augmented response to acoustic startle (Figure 6F), suggesting further deficits in processing sensorimotor stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from enhanced grip strength and acoustic startle responses.

claim: Injection of D1R selective agonist SKF38393 caused equal psychomotor activation in Pdcl cKO mice and their wild-type littermates.
source: Injection of mice with the D1R selective agonist SKF38393 that activates striatal neurons of the direct pathway caused equal psychomotor activation in Pdcl cKO mice and their wild-type littermates (Figure 6G).
evidence: Demonstrated by locomotor activity measurements after drug administration (Figure 6G).

claim: Administration of A2AR antagonist SCH58261 had no effect on the behavior of Pdcl cKO mice while significantly increasing locomotor activity of wild-type littermates.
source: In contrast, administration of A2AR antagonist SCH58261, that inhibits striatal neurons of the indirect pathway, had no effect on the behavior of Pdcl cKO mice while significantly increasing locomotor activity of wild-type littermates (Figure 6H).
evidence: Demonstrated by locomotor activity measurements after drug administration (Figure 6H).

claim: The D2R antagonist haloperidol induced catalepsy to a significantly greater extent in control littermates than in Pdcl cKO mice.
source: Conversely, the D2R antagonist haloperidol, that activates striatopallidal (indirect) pathway, induced catalepsy to a significantly greater extent in control littermates than in Pdcl cKO mice (Figure 6I).
evidence: Demonstrated by catalepsy measurements after drug administration (Figure 6I).

claim: The behavioral data suggest normal baseline behavior of Pdcl cKO mice with selective deficits in the striatal-mediated motor learning and sensorimotor coordination, preferentially affecting the function of the striatopallidal pathway.
source: In summary, the behavioral data suggest normal baseline behavior of Pdcl cKO mice with selective deficits in the striatal-mediated motor learning and sensorimotor coordination, preferentially affecting the function of the striatopallidal pathway.
evidence: Inferred from combined behavioral test results.

claim: AC5 is the major AC isoform in the striatum, accounting for ~ 80% of cAMP generation.
source: Striatal neurons receive diverse inputs that converge on AC5, the major AC isoform in the region, accounting for ~ 80% of cAMP generation (Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2002.

claim: Coupling of dopamine D1 and adenosine A2A receptors to increase cAMP production in striatal neurons is mediated to a large extent by a unique heterotrimer composed of Gαolf complexed with Gβ2 and Gγ7 subunits.
source: Coupling of key neurotransmitter receptors, such as dopamine D1 (D1R) and adenosine A2A (A2AR) to increase cAMP production in these neurons, is mediated to a large extent by a unique heterotrimer composed of the stimulatory α subunit Gαolf complexed with Gβ2 and Gγ7 subunits (Herve, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herve, 2011.

claim: Deletion of Gαolf, Gγ7 or AC5 in mice severely diminishes cAMP production in response to D1R and A2AR activation.
source: Indeed, deletion of Gαolf, Gγ7 or AC5 in mice severely diminishes cAMP production in response to D1R and A2AR activation, which is paralleled by muted behavioral responses to psychostimulants and antipsychotics that act on these receptors as well as by profound motor deficits (Corvol et al., 2007; Iwamoto et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2002; Sasaki et al., 2013; Schwindinger et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corvol et al., 2007; Iwamoto et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2002; Sasaki et al., 2013; Schwindinger et al., 2010.

claim: Mutations in Gαolf and AC5 have been shown to cause primary dystonia in humans.
source: Recently, mutations in Gαolf and AC5 have been shown to cause primary dystonia in humans (Carapito et al., 2014; Fuchs et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2014), further supporting the key contribution of Golf-AC5 signaling axis to pathophysiology of movement disorders.
evidence: Supported by citations to Carapito et al., 2014; Fuchs et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2014.

claim: Gαolf has lower efficiency of both receptor coupling and AC5 stimulation when tested in in vitro biochemical assays compared to Gαs.
source: Functionally, Gαolf is similar to another stimulatory G protein Gαs, but Gαolf has lower efficiency of both receptor coupling and AC5 stimulation when tested in in vitro biochemical assays (Chan et al., 2011; Jones et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chan et al., 2011; Jones et al., 1990.

claim: AC5 displays dual regulation by G protein subunits in which Gβγ acts to facilitate its activation by Gαs.
source: AC5 displays dual regulation by G protein subunits in which Gβγ acts to facilitate its activation by Gαs (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao et al., 2007.

claim: In vitro biochemical studies show that AC5 is capable of binding Gαs and Gβγ simultaneously.
source: In vitro biochemical studies show that AC5 is capable of binding Gαs and Gβγ simultaneously, suggesting that it can scaffold the stimulatory G protein heterotrimers (Sadana et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sadana et al., 2009.

claim: AC5 elimination leads to a reduction in expression levels of Gαolf in the striatum.
source: In mice, AC5 elimination leads to a reduction in expression levels of Gαolf in the striatum (Iwamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iwamoto et al., 2004.

claim: Knockout of Gγ7 reduces the expression of Gαolf and Gβ2.
source: Similarly, knockout of Gγ7 reduces the expression of Gαolf and Gβ2 (Sasaki et al., 2013; Schwindinger et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sasaki et al., 2013; Schwindinger et al., 2010.

claim: PhLP1 is required for the assembly of Gβ1 with Gαt1 and Gβ3 with Gαt2 as well as Gβ5 complexes with RGS9-1.
source: Previous in vivo studies also demonstrated that PhLP1 is required for the assembly of Gβ1 with Gαt1 and Gβ3 with Gαt2 as well as Gβ5 complexes with RGS9-1 (Lai et al., 2013, Tracy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lai et al., 2013 and Tracy et al., 2015.

claim: Deletion of PhLP1 in photoreceptors disrupts the formation of Gβ1γ1 (in rods), Gβ3γ8 (in cones) and Gβ5L/RGS9-1 complexes (in both rods and cones), dramatically decreasing their expression.
source: Consistent with this model, deletion of PhLP1 in photoreceptors disrupts the formation of Gβ1γ1 (in rods), Gβ3γ8 (in cones) and Gβ5L/RGS9-1 complexes (in both rods and cones), dramatically decreasing their expression (Lai et al., 2013; Tracy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lai et al., 2013 and Tracy et al., 2015.

claim: Overexpression of the dominant negative mutant of PhLP1 deficient in Gβ binding in rods down-regulates the expression of the Gβ1γ1 and Gβ5L/RGS9-1 complexes.
source: Similarly, overexpression of the dominant negative mutant of PhLP1 deficient in Gβ binding in rods down-regulates the expression of the Gβ1γ1 and Gβ5L/RGS9-1 complexes (Posokhova et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Posokhova et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of PhLP1 function results in a dramatic decrease in the expression of Gαt1 and Gαt2 subunits in rods and cones, respectively.
source: Interestingly, loss of PhLP1 function also results in a dramatic decrease in the expression of Gαt1 and Gαt2 subunits in rods and cones, respectively (Lai et al., 2013; Tracy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lai et al., 2013 and Tracy et al., 2015.

claim: Stability of Gαt1 and Gαt2 depends on their complex formation with Gβγ.
source: Given that stability of these Gα subunits depends on their complex formation with Gbg (Kolesnikov et al., 2011; Lobanova et al., 2008; Nikonov et al., 2013), the role of PhLP1 in stabilizing Gαt1 and Gαt2 is likely indirect and stems from its effects on Gβγ complex assembly.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kolesnikov et al., 2011; Lobanova et al., 2008; Nikonov et al., 2013.

claim: The assembly of AC5-Golf complex is mediated by PhLP1 chaperone that plays central role in neurotransmitter receptor coupling to cAMP production and motor learning.
source: We further identify that the assembly of AC5-Golf complex is mediated by PhLP1 chaperone that plays central role in neurotransmitter receptor coupling to cAMP production motor learning.
evidence: Inferred from combined results of molecular, biochemical, and behavioral studies.

claim: Elimination of PhLP1 in striatal neurons affects assembly and stability of the Golf-AC5 complex.
source: Elimination of PhLP1 in striatal neurons affects assembly and stability of the complex and causes selective impairment in sensorimotor behavior and motor skill learning, preferentially affecting signaling in the striatopallidal medium spiny neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by protein expression and behavioral studies in Pdcl cKO mice.

claim: Elimination of PhLP1 in striatal neurons causes selective impairment in sensorimotor behavior and motor skill learning.
source: Elimination of PhLP1 in striatal neurons affects assembly and stability of the complex and causes selective impairment in sensorimotor behavior and motor skill learning, preferentially affecting signaling in the striatopallidal medium spiny neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral studies in Pdcl cKO mice.

claim: Elimination of PhLP1 preferentially affects signaling in the striatopallidal medium spiny neurons.
source: Elimination of PhLP1 in striatal neurons affects assembly and stability of the complex and causes selective impairment in sensorimotor behavior and motor skill learning, preferentially affecting signaling in the striatopallidal medium spiny neurons.
evidence: Inferred from selective behavioral responses to drugs targeting indirect pathway.

claim: In the striatum, signaling via G protein-coupled neurotransmitter receptors is essential for motor control.
source: In the striatum, signaling via G protein-coupled neurotransmitter receptors is essential for motor control.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding of striatal function.

claim: The effector enzyme adenylyl cyclase type 5 (AC5) produces second messenger cAMP upon receptor-mediated activation by G protein Golf.
source: Critical to this process is the effector enzyme adenylyl cyclase type 5 (AC5) that produces second messenger cAMP upon receptor-mediated activation by G protein Golf.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding of AC5 function.

claim: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) form the largest group of the receptors responsible for the actions of the majority of neurotransmitters.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) form the largest group of the receptors responsible for the actions of the majority of neurotransmitters and play a critical role in virtually all neuronal functions (Gainetdinov et al., 2004; Wettschureck and Offermanns, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gainetdinov et al., 2004 and Wettschureck and Offermanns, 2005.

claim: Upon binding to neurotransmitter, GPCRs undergo conformational changes activating heterotrimeric G proteins by promoting GTP binding to Gα subunits and triggering the release of the Gβγ subunits.
source: In a classical model, upon binding to neurotransmitter, GPCRs undergo conformational changes activating heterotrimeric G proteins by promoting GTP binding to Gα subunits and triggering the release of the Gβγ subunits.
evidence: Describes classical model of GPCR signaling from established scientific knowledge.

claim: When dissociated, both Gα and Gβγ subunits modulate the activities of downstream effector molecules.
source: When dissociated, both Gα and Gβγ subunits modulate the activities of downstream effector molecules that are directly responsible for generating cellular responses (Gilman, 1987; Neer, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gilman, 1987 and Neer, 1995.

claim: An emerging alternative model suggests that G protein heterotrimers exist in more stable complexes that rearrange rather than dissociate upon activation.
source: However, an emerging alternative model suggests that G protein heterotrimers exist in more stable complexes that rearrange rather than dissociate upon activation and may further form higher order signaling complexes with receptors and effectors (Bunemann et al., 2003; Dupre et al., 2009; Hepler, 2014; Lambert, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bunemann et al., 2003; Dupre et al., 2009; Hepler, 2014; Lambert, 2008.

claim: Several chaperone proteins have been described to be required for the biogenesis of the G protein subunits and their complexes.
source: Indeed, several chaperone proteins have been described to be required for the biogenesis of the G protein subunits and their complexes (Dupre et al., 2009; Papasergi et al., 2015; Willardson and Tracy, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dupre et al., 2009; Papasergi et al., 2015; Willardson and Tracy, 2012.

claim: Adenylyl cyclase (AC) is an enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of the second messenger cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).
source: One of the central and best studied G protein effectors is adenylyl cyclase (AC), an enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of the second messenger cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) (Taussig and Gilman, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taussig and Gilman, 1995.

claim: Numerous isoforms of AC are differentially modulated by both Gβγ and various Gα-GTP subunits.
source: Numerous isoforms of AC are differentially modulated by both Gβγ and various Gα-GTP subunits and play critical roles in a variety of fundamental neuronal processes (Sadana and Dessauer, 2009; Sunahara et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sadana and Dessauer, 2009 and Sunahara et al., 1996.

claim: The striatum is the input structure of the basal ganglia circuit essential for initiating and maintaining movement, mood control, and reward valuation.
source: GPCR signaling to AC performs a particularly important function in the striatum, the input structure of the basal ganglia circuit essential for initiating and maintaining movement, mood control, and reward valuation (Graybiel, 2000; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Graybiel, 2000 and Kreitzer and Malenka, 2008.

claim: Imbalance in cAMP homeostasis in the striatum has been associated with drug addiction, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and a variety of movement disorders.
source: Imbalance in cAMP homeostasis in this region has been associated with drug addiction, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and a variety of movement disorders (Bonito-Oliva et al., 2011; Girault, 2012; Nestler and Aghajanian, 1997; Wilson and Brandon, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonito-Oliva et al., 2011; Girault, 2012; Nestler and Aghajanian, 1997; Wilson and Brandon, 2015.

claim: PhLP1 is thought to function as a co-chaperone with the cytosolic chaperonin complex (CCT), assisting in retrieval of the Gβ subunits emerging from the CCT and presenting them for the association with the Gg subunits.
source: It is thought to function as a co-chaperone with the cytosolic chaperonin complex (CCT), assisting in retrieval of the Gβ subunits emerging from the CCT and presenting them for the association with the Gg subunits (Willardson and Tracy, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Willardson and Tracy, 2012.

claim: PhLP1 chaperones the formation of complexes involving the atypical Gβ5 subunits and the Gγ-like domains in RGS proteins.
source: In addition to assisting folding of conventional Gβγ complexes, PhLP1 chaperones the formation of the structurally similar complexes involving the atypical Gβ5 subunits and the Gγ-like domains in RGS proteins (Howlett et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howlett et al., 2009.

claim: This study is the first to document a case in which stable association with all subunits of G protein heterotrimer is required for the stability of an effector.
source: While there are several examples for the association of both Gα and Gβγ subunits with effector molecule, e.g. PLCβ, GIRK channels, AC isoforms (Kovoor and Lester, 2002; Lyon et al., 2014; Sunahara et al., 1996), to the best of our knowledge this study is the first to document a case in which stable association with all subunits of G protein heterotrimer is required for the stability of an effector.
evidence: Claimed as novel finding based on comparison with existing literature.

claim: In striatal neurons heterotrimeric Golf-AC5 is assembled in a pre-coupled 'signalosome' in which subunits rearrange rather than physically dissociate upon GPCR activation.
source: Taken together with biochemical studies showing that AC5 is capable of scaffolding inactive G protein heterotrimers (Sadana et al., 2009), our results suggest that in striatal neurons heterotrimeric Golf-AC5 is assembled in a pre-coupled 'signalosome' in which subunits rearrange rather than physically dissociate upon GPCR activation.
evidence: Inferred from combined results of this study and supported by citation to Sadana et al., 2009.

claim: PhLP1 directly binds to Gβγ subunits.
source: Given that PhLP1 directly binds to Gbg subunits (Savage et al., 2000b; Thibault et al., 1997) and has been shown to be required for folding Gβ2γ7 in transfected cells (Howlett et al., 2009), we propose the following model for the role in PhLP1 the assembly of the Golf-AC5 complex.
evidence: Supported by citations to Savage et al., 2000b and Thibault et al., 1997.

claim: PhLP1 has been shown to be required for folding Gβ2γ7 in transfected cells.
source: Given that PhLP1 directly binds to Gbg subunits (Savage et al., 2000b; Thibault et al., 1997) and has been shown to be required for folding Gβ2γ7 in transfected cells (Howlett et al., 2009), we propose the following model for the role in PhLP1 the assembly of the Golf-AC5 complex.
evidence: Supported by citation to Howlett et al., 2009.

claim: PhLP1 assists the assembly of the Gβ2γ7 complex, increasing its expression, which in turn upregulates Gαolf, and higher levels of Gαolfβ2γ7 promote stabilization of AC5 by forming pre-coupled complexes with it.
source: PhLP1 assists the assembly of the Gβ2γ7 complex, increasing its expression, which in turn upregulates Gαolf. Higher levels of Gαolfβ2γ7 promote stabilization of the AC5 by forming pre-coupled complexes with it.
evidence: Proposed model based on combined experimental results.

claim: PhLP1 triggers a chain of events resulting in the stabilization of the entire AC5-Golf complex ensuring its high expression level and setting the stoichiometry.
source: Thus, PhLP1 triggers a chain of events resulting in the stabilization of the entire AC5-Golf complex ensuring its high expression level and setting the stoichiometry (Figure 7).
evidence: Proposed model based on combined experimental results and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Studies in transfected cells indicate that PhLP1 participates in folding and stabilization of virtually all Gβγ combinations including complexes of Gβ5 with RGS9 and RGS7.
source: Studies in transfected cells indicate that PhLP1 participates in folding and stabilization of virtually all Gβγ combinations including complexes of Gβ5 with RGS9 and RGS7 (Howlett et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howlett et al., 2009.

claim: PhLP1 elimination has no effect on the expression of Gβ1 in the striatum, a subunit clearly impacted by PhLP1 loss in rod photoreceptors.
source: Yet, we find that in the striatum, PhLP1 elimination has no effect on the expression of many G protein subunits, including Gβ1, a subunit clearly impacted by PhLP1 loss in rod photoreceptors (Lai et al., 2013).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting (Figure 5B) and supported by citation to Lai et al., 2013.

claim: PhLP1 action may be the rate-limiting factor required for achieving high expression of G proteins with abundant mRNA expression in a particular neuronal population.
source: In this scenario, PhLP1 action may be the rate-limiting factor required for achieving high expression of G proteins with abundant mRNA expression in a particular neuronal population, e.g. Gαt1β1γ1, Gαt2β3γ8 and Gαolfβ2γ7 overexpressed in rods, cones and striatal neurons, respectively.
evidence: Proposed explanation for selective effects of PhLP1 loss.

claim: The Golf heterotrimer is essential for coupling both D1 and A2A receptors in direct and indirect striatal neurons to stimulation of cAMP production.
source: The Golf heterotrimer is known to be essential for coupling both D1 and A2A receptors in direct and indirect striatal neurons to stimulation of cAMP production (Herve, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Herve, 2011.

claim: Knockout of Gnal or Gng7 markedly reduces the ability of D1R and A2AR agonists to increase cAMP.
source: Knockout of Gnal or Gng7 that encode Gαolf or Gγ7 respectively, markedly reduces the ability of D1R and A2AR agonists to increase cAMP, and this biochemical observation is paralleled by muted behavioral responses of mice to psychostimulants that activate these receptors (Corvol et al., 2001; Schwindinger et al., 2003; Zhuang et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corvol et al., 2001; Schwindinger et al., 2003; Zhuang et al., 2000.

claim: Acute psychomotor responses to drugs appear to be particularly sensitive to loss of Golf, while adaptive behaviors to repeated drug exposure are preserved.
source: Acute psychomotor responses to drugs appear to be particularly sensitive to loss of Golf, while adaptive behaviors to repeated drug exposure are preserved (Corvol et al., 2007; Schwindinger et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corvol et al., 2007 and Schwindinger et al., 2010.

claim: Gαolf haploinsufficiency leads to selective deficits in cAMP signaling without detrimentally affecting coupling to ERK.
source: For example, while Gαolf is critical for the ability of D1R to stimulate both cAMP production and ERK phosphorylation, Gαolf haploinsufficiency leads to selective deficits in cAMP signaling without detrimentally affecting coupling to ERK (Corvol et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Corvol et al., 2007.

claim: AC5 mediates nearly 80% of cAMP increase in response to D1R and A2AR activation.
source: Although, activation of either D1R and A2A clearly results in the increase in cAMP levels (Corvol et al., 2001; Iwamoto et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2002) and AC5 mediates nearly 80% of this effect (Lee et al., 2002), elimination of AC5 in mice does not diminish behavioral responses of mice to the administration of A1R and D1R agonists (Iwamoto et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2002.

claim: Elimination of AC5 in mice does not diminish behavioral responses to the administration of A2AR and D1R agonists.
source: Although, activation of either D1R and A2A clearly results in the increase in cAMP levels (Corvol et al., 2001; Iwamoto et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2002) and AC5 mediates nearly 80% of this effect (Lee et al., 2002), elimination of AC5 in mice does not diminish behavioral responses of mice to the administration of A1R and D1R agonists (Iwamoto et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Iwamoto et al., 2003 and Lee et al., 2002.

claim: Mice lacking AC5 have abolished responses to D2 antagonists.
source: At the same time, mice lacking AC5 have abolished responses to D2 antagonists, suggesting greater impact of signaling via AC5 in indirect pathway neurons (Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2002.

claim: Balance of neurotransmitter signaling between direct and indirect pathway striatal neurons sets a tightly orchestrated coordination of movements.
source: Balance of neurotransmitter signaling between direct and indirect pathway striatal neurons is thought to set a tightly orchestrated coordination of movements (Graybiel, 2005; Nelson and Kreitzer, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Graybiel, 2005 and Nelson and Kreitzer, 2014.

claim: Mice lacking AC5 or Gγ7 show profound deficits in motor learning and coordination.
source: In agreement with this idea, mice lacking AC5 or Gγ7 show profound deficits in motor learning and coordination (Iwamoto et al., 2003; Kheirbek et al., 2009; Sasaki et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Iwamoto et al., 2003; Kheirbek et al., 2009; Sasaki et al., 2013.

claim: Preservation of D1R mediated behavioral responses in Pdcl cKO mice may indicate that signaling pathways other than cAMP initiated by D1 receptors play compensatory role.
source: Alternatively, preservation of D1R mediated behavioral responses in Pdcl cKO mice may also indicate that signaling pathways other than cAMP initiated by D1 receptors (Nishi et al., 2011) play compensatory role.
evidence: Proposed explanation for observed results, supported by citation to Nishi et al., 2011.

claim: The study introduces PhLP1 as a critical regulator of Golf-AC5 complex assembly and an interesting molecular player to consider in the pathology of dystonia and possibly other movement disorders.
source: In any event, our study demonstrates the importance of proper Golf-AC5 complex expression and assembly for the balance of the neurotransmitter signaling in striatal neurons and introduces PhLP1 as a critical regulator of the process and an interesting molecular player to consider in the pathology of dystonia and possibly other movement disorders.
evidence: Inferred from combined results of the study.
